The paper offers a perspective on regional allocation of human capital and skill mismatch by
discussing different strands of the literature (human capital theory, economic geography,
education policy, institutions, etc.) and showing complementary empirical evidence using variation
in the location quotient index. The index is based on education shares across three broad
occupational groups in NUTS2 regions from a selected group of countries. The authors document
considerable regional variation in skill mismatch.
Overall, I found the paper thought-provoking and I appreciated that it drew upon various
literatures. However, I am unsure that it is possible to adequately address all questions raised by
the paper within the analysis framework chosen by the authors. More specific comments follow.
i) The paper does not separate normative from positive statements in a clear way, while lacking
notion of an optimal allocation of talent without which such discussion cannot be done. In the
empirical part, the authors focus on vertical mismatch, by which they implicitly mean high skilled
workers employed in non-managerial and non-professional roles (ISCO groups below 3). However,
such allocation could arise due to a particular industry structure which favours middle-skilled
occupations and therefore attracts a disproportionate amount of workers across all skill levels.
The paper could be improved by separating the issues of spatial allocation from mismatch, and by
corroborating the results on mismatch by other indicators of skill shortages and oversupply, such
as rates of return to education, local unemployment rates and job turnover.
ii) The authors' construction of the quotient index assumes that all countries should have similar
relative shares of human capital allocation, but this ignores country-level differences in education
systems organisation and differences in economic development (as more developed economies
tend to have higher investment rates in education in general). For example, vocational education
plays a relatively larger role in Germany and provides educational tracks to occupations which
would otherwise require a college degree in other countries. Since such country-level differences
make the results difficult to interpret, the authors should focus on within-country variation.

iii) While the paper introduces five different factors of regional specialisation, the empirical
approach doesn't in fact leave the realm of the neoclassical human capital theory, as it is largely
informed by spatial allocation of workers within the standard labour demand framework with
regional specialisation. While the authors mention other determinants such as global value chains
and local institutions, there is no systematic characterisation of their variation shown with data.
The findings on mismatch in particular lack an interpretation supported by documented evidence
on country and regional differences along the dimensions considered in the paper. Given
limitations of regional data, it is doubtful that it is feasible to discuss all these mechanisms in
detail and isolate their effects. However, the paper can still be informative by developing
comprehensive descriptive evidence in a systematic way.
iv) The paper omits critical details about the sample construction: it is not clear whether the
authors imposed age restrictions, used only full-time or part-time workers, included both genders
or only males, included or excluded migrant workers (which can have strong implications for the
results). It's also not clear whether nation averages of the shares are weighted. How did the
authors handle missing data?
v) I am concerned about specific years chosen for the analysis (2009, 2021) which could affect the
results due to strong negative economic shocks which were unevenly distributed. Since the
analysis doesn't rely on time variation, the authors should use different years and average the
results across 5 or 10 year intervals to reduce noise.
vi) The paper only shows the results for high skilled workers. What about other groups?

This article approaches a very interesting and important topic: the geography of skill mismatches
in Europe. The article uses quantitative data to map skill mismatches in selected regions, and
discusses reasons as to why these geographical variations arise.
In fact, it would benefit the article if it could focus even more on this phenomenon and its
explanations. The introduction is interesting because it juxtaposes more traditional human capital
theory with arguments derived from geographical political economy. However, while one could
debate the outcomes of this intellectual tension, this is not really the core of the article (human
capital theory is though dismissed as simplistic and positivist – a language I would myself avoid
given the convincing literature on the overall benefits of education and higher skills). The focus of
the article is not to estimate the benefits from education. Instead, I would wish for a stronger
focus on the geography of skill mismatches in the introduction. This also would open to the real
empirical geographical question in the article – what does the geography of skill mismatches look
like, and why do differences between regions arise across Europe?
I would also recommend a revision of the literature review in the same fashion (section: Human
capital and its uneven spatial distribution). Right now, this section focuses on human capital
theory and some sources of mismatches. The discussion makes a valid point around the
importance of institutions (in fact, one could probably argue that labour market and education
institutions are among the most variable factors across the countries within the single market).
Moreover, the geographical discussion treats the issue of regional divergence and uneven
regional development. On this topic, there is already a sizeable literature, and this should also not
be the core discussion of this paper. While I would actually like to challenge some of the
arguments in a within-European context (for example, that growth is a trade-off between regions,
the peculiar connection made between vocational training and precarious labour and the new
rounds of “Fordist-influenced spatial organization” – within Europe the Fordist era was in fact
characterized by decreasing regional economic disparities), this is besides the point.
Instead, I would like to recommend a stronger focus on the geographies of mismatches and why
they arise. The paper would make a stronger contribution if it could remain with this focus. In
particular, I would welcome a discussion about the dimensions that the authors later return to as
explaining the geography of mismatches: dynamism of national economies, regional
specializations, local institutions and demographic structure. In such a context, for example, the
discussion about the global production chains and their spatialities is interesting, but it does not
quite explain the geography of mismatches.

In the empirical part, the use of the different LQs is ingenious. However, it would be great if the
authors could comment on the reliability of the mismatch indicator: is there a risk that we simply
misjudged the level of skills needed in jobs, or that they changed? And where in the economy do
the most important mismatches arise? I believe that this could be easily described using the
available data, as an introduction to the geographical analysis. It would also be good if the authors
explained whether the patterns could be taken to be general – or are the results a feature of the
regions/countries that selected themselves into the university initiative?
The authors caution a warning for fig. 1.1a and b. It is hard what to make of this – is this part of
the analysis reliable or not?
In the discussion section, the authors are looking for different ways to explain the geographical
variation in the mismatches. It would be good to know how the authors ended up thinking about
these factors (linking to the theoretical section above). Secondly, it is a bit hard for the reader to
evaluate the relevance of the factors. Here, I would recommend the authors to provide empirical
evidence. If not in terms of regressions, so at least displaying the co-variation between the factors
and mismatches in regions. For example, one could display a scatterplot between the size of the
mismatch in regions, and the demographic structure. I believe that relevant indicators could be
calculated for all the dimensions. Such an exercise would make the arguments much more
convincing and interesting.
To complement this, we should always keep in mind that the LQs illustrate the spatial variation of
a phenomenon (relative), and not how important the phenomenon itself is (absolute). In fact, it
would be good to know the absolute level too – how sizeable are the mismatches around
European regions? This would be a way to illustrate the absolute importance of the phenomenon.
Also, but this is maybe too much of an extension, it would be very interesting to know if the
mismatches actually have consequences for regional growth (or, are the mismatches rather a
result of growth because growing regions attract labour that maybe cannot be accommodated
immediately?). Using the lag structure of the data, such an experiment could be made.
In the policy recommendations, the authors argue for “strong interventions”. However, the
interventions that they mention seem to be only vaguely related to the findings of this paper
(except maybe for the high-quality career counselling). Instead, I would encourage the authors to
develop policy recommendations that are immediately associated with the findings of this paper.
In sum, I find the topic and empirical approach very promising. However, revisions according to
the above would give the paper a much stronger basis to argue for particular and precise
conclusions concerning the geography of skill mismatches in the European Union. I do hope that
the authors find these comments constructive for further work.

Dear Reviewer, we would like to thank you for your valuable and insightful comments. We
have proceeded with major revisions on our manuscript, following most of your points,
which we found well raised. These changes have bolstered our arguments, slightly
extending the text’s wording, without changing its meaning. Please find below our
responses to your comments in detail.
Reviewer: The paper does not separate normative from positive statements in a clear
way, while lacking the notion of an optimal allocation of talent without which such
discussion cannot be done.
Author Response: To address the first part of this crucial comment, we rephrased various
sections of the manuscript. Now, observations based on empirical evidence are clearly
stated, allowing the reader to easily distinguish them from statements which express our
opinions. Regarding the lack of the notion of an optimal allocation of talent, we have revised
the Theoretical and Conceptual Section of our manuscript. Specifically, in this section we
open a whole part where we discuss the factors shaping the uneven geography of skill
mismatches writing that: “To maximize the effects of higher educational attainment, however,
talent has to be allocated in an optimal way, namely, a worker must employ their skills in the
most appropriate setting. It is then through the optimal allocation of talent that a higher
educational attainment level generates individual and social returns (Acemoglu, 1995).” Further
below, the concept is scrutinized in detail, using the appropriate literature. Then, in the
Discussion, the concept now plays a key role.
In the empirical part, the authors focus on vertical mismatch, by which they implicitly
mean high skilled workers employed in non-managerial and non-professional roles
(ISCO groups below 3). However, such allocation could arise due to a particular
industry structure which favours middle-skilled occupations and therefore attracts a
disproportionate amount of workers across all skill levels. The paper could be
improved by separating the issues of spatial allocation from mismatch, and by
corroborating the results on mismatch by other indicators of skill shortages and
oversupply, such as rates of return to education, local unemployment rates and job
turnover.
Author Response: This is a well raised point. However, due to limited space, we could not
address both the issues of mismatches’ spatial allocation as well as the nature of vertical
mismatches. Unavoidably, we relied on secondary data that do not consider the qualitative
aspects of these vertical mismatches. Nevertheless, we linked the concentration of various
types of skill (mis)matches with a series of factors, including through macroeconomic,
population, innovation, and demographic indicators. Please refer to our response to
Comment 8 by Reviewer 1. The issue of particular industry structures which favour middleskilled occupations is addressed in the Discussion. Indicatively, we write: “Apart from
tourism, there are many manufacturing- and assembly-related activities along GVCs that favor
medium skill-level occupations and therefore generate tendencies towards a disproportionate

amount of highly educated workers in such occupations. Such is the case with most French
regions, and especially the agri-food heavy Franche-Comté.”
While the paper introduces five different factors of regional specialisation, the
empirical approach doesn't in fact leave the realm of the neoclassical human capital
theory, as it is largely informed by spatial allocation of workers within the standard
labour demand framework with regional specialisation. While the authors mention
other determinants such as global value chains and local institutions, there is no
systematic characterisation of their variation shown with data. The findings on
mismatch in particular lack an interpretation supported by documented evidence on
country and regional differences along the dimensions considered in the paper. Given
limitations of regional data, it is doubtful that it is feasible to discuss all these
mechanisms in detail and isolate their effects. However, the paper can still be
informative by developing comprehensive descriptive evidence in a systematic way.
Author Response: It is correctly stated that limitations of regional data, as well as the
paper’s word limitation, did not allow us to make our postulations regarding GVCs more
evidence-based. Nevertheless, we addressed your comment by developing comprehensive
descriptive evidence in a systematic way around the five factors inquired in the Discussion.
Specifically, our Empirical Analysis now provides concrete evidence for our postulations in
the Discussion by including a scrutiny of indicators on GDP, innovation performance,
population density, and demographic structures. Please refer to our response to Comment
8 by Reviewer 1 for more detail regarding the proxies that we used and the methods we
implemented for their analysis. Moreover, all these factors are covered in the Theoretical
and Conceptual Section as well. Please refer to our response to Comment 3 by Reviewer 2
for more detail.
The authors' construction of the quotient index assumes that all countries should
have similar relative shares of human capital allocation, but this ignores country-level
differences in education systems organisation and differences in economic
development (as more developed economies tend to have higher investment rates in
education in general). For example, vocational education plays a relatively larger role
in Germany and provides educational tracks to occupations which would otherwise
require a college degree in other countries. Since such country-level differences make
the results difficult to interpret, the authors should focus on within-country variation.
Author Response: Although this is a well raised point, the main goal of our analysis was to
directly compare the performance of various EU regions in terms of addressing skill
mismatches. For that reason, we went with the relative-to-transnational LQ as our main
index. Nevertheless, we accept that structural differences between countries make such
comparisons a difficult case. Apart from the latter, we are perfectly aware that the LQ can
sometimes lead to contradicting results due to not providing a clear view of the absolute
magnitude of the phenomenon under study, or due to the modifiable areal unit problem. To
overcome all the above, we tried to consider a wide array of country-specific factors when
discussing our findings. For instance, we have extensively relied on relevant research
around the employment/educational regimes typology. For instance, we write in the revised
Theoretical and Conceptual Section: “Nevertheless, dual educational systems such as Germany’s
have also been praised for their positive effects in school-to-work transitions, albeit having been
oversimplified in the relevant literature (Deissinger, 2015). Similarly praised is the universalistic

regime in Nordic countries like Denmark, which invest in human capital and match high levels of
educational attainment with demand for such workers (Hadjivassiliou et al., 2019). [...] …in statist
regimes, for instance, employers are not sufficiently involved in matching skills’ demand and
supply (Capsada-Munsech & Valiente, 2020). As such, in the sub-protective regime of the
Mediterranean EU, in countries like Greece, youth transitions to adulthood are long and
problematic (Emmanouil et al., 2023). This leads to a large pool of highly qualified people who
either cannot find a job, have a profession for which they are overqualified, or have a profession
in a different sector from the one in which they were trained, while at the same time many
companies are struggling to fill their vacancies (Biagi et al., 2020).” Similarly, in the Discussion
we write: “...the universalistic (e.g.Denmark) regime with high investments in education and fast
and stable school-to-work transitions is completely different from countries of the sub-protective
regime (e.g. Greece), which display severe skills mismatches and low labour demand in general
(Hadjivassiliou et al., 2019).”.
The paper omits critical details about the sample construction: it is not clear whether
the authors imposed age restrictions, used only full-time or part-time workers,
included both genders or only males, included or excluded migrant workers (which
can have strong implications for the results). It's also not clear whether nation
averages of the shares are weighted. How did the authors handle missing data?
Author Response: To address this comment, we have added to the Methodological Section
that “Eurostat’s sample covers all employed persons of both genders, aged 15 and above. Data
imputation methods were not used, given that the extent of missing data is limited and most
missing values refer to a specific type of skill mismatch (highly educated workers in low skill-level
occupations), making most such methods unreliable.”
I am concerned about specific years chosen for the analysis (2009, 2021) which could
affect the results due to strong negative economic shocks which were unevenly
distributed. Since the analysis doesn't rely on time variation, the authors should use
different years and average the results across 5 or 10 year intervals to reduce noise.
Author Response: This is another excellent point which could lead to very interesting
findings. In practical terms, we could add one or two years between 2009 and 2021.
However, this could substantially add to the wordage of the manuscript. Moreover, we
believe that the years under study as it is allow for a comparison between two crucial
moments in the EU’s recent history: the onset of a period of successive crises and the onset
of a period of a renewed round of pandemic- and geopolitically-induced crises. Moreover,
please note that our analysis, given that the LQ is a relative indicator, avoids looking into
the changes in the extent of skill mismatches between 2009 and 2021. Relatedly, we note in
the Empirical Analysis Section: “It must be noted that the LQ is a relative index, meaning that its
changes over time do not indicate neither absolute growth nor retraction of the phenomenon
under study. Therefore, correlations pertaining to LQ changes over time must be approached
with caution.” As such, we believe that the noise does not affect the significance of our
observations considerably.

have proceeded with major revisions on our manuscript, following most of your points,
which we found well raised. These changes have bolstered our arguments, slightly
extending the text’s wording, without changing its meaning. Please find below our
responses to your comments in detail.

and discusses reasons as to why these geographical variations arise. In fact, it

This is a well raised point. In the revised version of the manuscript, we clarify our
empirically-grounded positioning in relation to the HCT. Overall, we try to show that a
fruitful synthesis of notions from HCT with notions from GPE can be a very illuminating
theoretical and practical exercise that sheds light on the deeper factors driving skill
mismatches. Apart from the above, we follow your suggestion and enhance our focus on

the uneven geography of skill mismatches. In doing so, we have advanced the aim and the
specific questions in the Introduction but also have adapted the subsequent sections
accordingly. Especially in the Theoretical and Conceptual Section, we now focus more on the
socio-spatial drivers of skill mismatches and explain the reasons why geographical
variations arise. This is detailed when addressing your second point. Lastly, in the
Introduction we put more emphasis on what the EU is doing to address skill mismatches.
1. On this topic, there is already a sizeable literature, and this should also not be
the core discussion of this paper. While I would actually like to challenge some
of the arguments in a within-European context (for example, that growth is a
trade-off between regions, the peculiar connection made between vocational
training and precarious labour and the new rounds of “Fordist-influenced spatial
organization” – within Europe the Fordist era was in fact characterized by
decreasing regional economic disparities), this is besides the point. Instead, I
would like to recommend a stronger focus on the geographies of mismatches
and why they arise. The paper would make a stronger contribution if it could
remain with this focus. In particular, I would welcome a discussion about the
dimensions that the authors later return to as explaining the geography of
mismatches: dynamism of national economies, regional specializations, local
institutions and demographic structure. In such a context, for example, the
discussion about the global production chains and their spatialities is
interesting, but it does not quite explain the geography of mismatches.
This is another well raised point that we have taken into account in our revisions.
Specifically, the Theoretical and Conceptual Section has been extensively revised so as to
follow a clear narrative revolving around the uneven geography of skill mismatches. In this
section then, we now present some basic points raised in the literature regarding the
factors underlying this uneven geography; to do so, we have added numerous new sources.
As you stressed, most of these points pertain to the factors that are inquired in the
Discussion Section (dynamism of national economies, regional productive priorities,
institutional endowments, urbanization levels, etc.). To deepen this Section’s clear targeting,
we have also taken out a good part of the postulations regarding the effect of Fordism on
uneven development, as well as the role of global value chains. The same principle is
followed in the Discussion.
1. In the empirical part, the use of the different LQs is ingenious. However, it
would be great if the authors could comment on the reliability of the mismatch
indicator: is there a risk that we simply misjudged the level of skills needed in
jobs, or that they changed?
To clarify the source for our calculated LQs, we now stress in the Methodological Section:
“Data on the matching between highly educated workers and low, medium, and high skill-level
occupations are directly calculated by Eurostat, based on its Labour Force Survey.” Further
below, we now add in regard to the reliability of the mismatch indicator: “The classification of
skill levels was carried out at our request by Eurostat itself, to eliminate the risk of misjudging
skill levels and to increase the reliability of the mismatch index.” It should be clear then, that the
shares of highly educated workers per skill-level occupation at the regional level were
directly provided to us by Eurostat. Of course, Eurostat’s methodology carries some
inherent weaknesses, such as that skill mismatches are judged solely based on the
correspondence between a worker’s education attainment level (following the ISCED
typology) and an occupation’s demanded skill level (following the ISCO typology). No

qualitative dimensions are then taken into account; but this is a shortcoming characterizing
most—if not all—secondary analyses on skill mismatches (as noted by several experts in the
literature; e.g., see MacGuinness et al., 2018).
1. And where in the economy do the most important mismatches arise? I believe
that this could be easily described using the available data, as an introduction to
the geographical analysis.
We must note that this is another well raised point that would lead to very interesting
findings. However, we have not inquired about skill mismatches by sector, for two main
reasons. First, for reasons of data limitations. After checking the available data, analysis per
sector and region would have to rely on really small samples which would not be reliable.
This is stated in the Methodology Section: “...as the focus of this paper is on the regional level,
our analysis cannot include skill mismatches by sector and region, given that this would lead to
extensive data fragmentation and therefore to issues of reliability and missing values.” Secondly,
a sectoral analysis would require the addition of substantial text, which would make the
manuscript even lengthier. Therefore, we deemed that a sectoral analysis—albeit
interesting—lies outside the scope of our paper. Nevertheless, we have included relevant
insight from the literature in the Theoretical and Conceptual Section, and then revisit this
insight in the Discussion. Specifically, in the former section we write: “...apart from the
dynamism of a regional industrial structure, the sectoral specialization per se plays a key role.
Characteristically, sectors like accommodation and catering, commerce and storage, and
transportation, are reported to suffer greater skill mismatches—both horizontal and
vertical—than others (Chłoń-Domińczak & Żurawski, 2017).”
1. It would also be good if the authors explained whether the patterns could be
taken to be general – or are the results a feature of the regions/countries that
selected themselves into the university initiative?
Although our study focuses mainly on the ERUA regions and countries, our findings can be
considered more broadly. We state the reason for this in the Methodological Section, which
is that the countries under study were chosen not only because of the ReERUA Project, but
also because they represent all key educational/employment regimes in Europe. Specifically,
we write: “The analysis is conducted at the regional level (NUTS-2) and its geographical scope
covers five countries: Greece, Bulgaria, France, Germany, and Denmark. These were chosen on
the basis that they represent the main educational/employment regimes in Europe: the
universalistic of the Nordic countries, the employment-centered of Continental Europe, the subprotective of the Mediterranean countries, and the post-socialist of Eastern Europe (Pohl &
Walther 2007; Farkas, 2011). While both France and Germany fall under the Continental model,
they are both analyzed due to their stark differences in terms of their wage structures (Hein &
Vogel, 2009) and educational models (O’Reilly et al., 2019). Given the research’s geographical
scope covering all main European regimes pertaining to employment and skills, its findings can
be contextualized more broadly and provide insight into the EU as a whole.” The above is also
implied in the Introduction and the Discussion.
1. The authors caution a warning for fig. 1.1a and b. It is hard what to make of this
– is this part of the analysis reliable or not?
This is an extremely important point. To address it and secure the reliability of our analysis,
we now clarify in the Empirical Analysis Section that: “Paradoxically, in both Figures 2a and 2b,
LQ scores fluctuate exclusively above 1, indicating over-concentrations in all regions for which
data were available. The reason for this is because the phenomenon of highly educated workers
being employed in low skill-level occupations is inherently limited. As a result, regions with a

small number of such workers, which would exhibit LQ scores below 1, have a non-statistically
significant sample, thus data for them is missing. Conversely, the available data allows for
observing where highly educated workers are over-concentrated in low skill-level occupations.” In
other words, our observations regarding where highly educated workers in low skill-level
occupations are concentrated, we follow a process of elimination. Namely, although we do
not have sufficient data to directly observe which regions exhibit under-concentration of
this type of skill mismatch, we systematically exclude all other possibilities based on the
available data, and we are left with the answer to our problem.
1. In the discussion section, the authors are looking for different ways to explain
the geographical variation in the mismatches. It would be good to know how
the authors ended up thinking about these factors.
To address this comment, we have revised several sections of our manuscript. In short, we
can state here that we ended up with these based on the insight of the relevant literature.
This was the case from the start; however, it is a fact that this was not adequately clarified in
our initial submission. Thus, including them in the Theoretical and Conceptual Section was
crucial. Doing so, we cover the literature around the role of the dynamism of national
economies in skills’ geography in a paragraph starting with: “Various factors shape the widely
documented uneven geography of skills and their mismatches (Alamá-Sabater et al., 2024;
Cedefop, 2010). Importantly, regional mismatches can be greatly affected by the robustness (or
lack thereof) of the broader national economy.” Similarly, we write about the effect of regional
specializations: “At the regional level, the dynamism of an economy is equally crucial. Capitaland technology-intensive activities tend to concentrate in already advanced regions, fueling new
rounds of uneven development (Vinuela-Jimenez et al., 2010). As such, metropolitan areas with a
diverse economic base concentrate human capital, cutting-edge technology, and finance-related
activities, while economically backward and declining regions become even more disconnected
from knowledge and innovation (Feldman et al., 2021). Similarly, developed industrial regions
tend to attract new activities, workforce, and capital, as they further industrialise (Boudeville,
1968), although in many cases they also spill over positive effects to their surrounding areas
(Perroux, 1955).” The role of institutional endowments is scrutinized throughout this section,
as for instance in the part we write: “Such segmentation is crucially sustained by dual human
capital development mechanisms. Namely, next to a robust education system, a training system
that focuses more on vocational training and apprenticeship initiatives is formed, serving as a
channel for precarious labour (Teixeira, 2019).” Apart from the above, we lay out the relevant
literature’s insight into the effect of crises of various types on the geography of skill
mismatches in the paragraph starting with: “Beyond the national and regional factors, sudden
shocks of economic or other nature, as well as structural transitions, directly contribute to
increasing skill mismatches (Cedefop, 2015).” The latter is particularly important in justifying
our rationale behind the temporal scope of our paper covering a period of successive crises.
Then, in the Empirical Analysis these crucial factors are scrutinized through a series of
correlations between our LQs and proxies. Relatedly, we state in the Methodological
Section: “Regarding the correlation analysis, the research at hand statistically associates the LQ
values of the above analysis with crucial factors underlying the geographical allocation of skills
as noted in the relevant literature (e.g. Cedefop, 2010). Specifically, it links the LQL, LQM, and LQH
with regional and national GDP (both total and per capita), the European Commission’s Regional
Innovation Index, urbanization levels, the Ageing Index, and the Dependency Index (see Table 1).”
Further below, in the beginning of Discussion, we stress this again: “Drawing upon our main
findings, here we discuss the most crucial factors underlying the uneven geography of skill

mismatches. In this framework, we put particular emphasis on the economic dynamism of
national economies, regional industrial structures, urbanization, local institutional structures and
practices, and demographic structures, drawing from the main findings of the relevant literature
(Alamá-Sabater, 2024; Cedefop, 2010).”
1. Secondly, it is a bit hard for the reader to evaluate the relevance of the factors.
Here, I would recommend the authors to provide empirical evidence. If not in
terms of regressions, so at least displaying the co-variation between the factors
and mismatches in regions. For example, one could display a scatterplot
between the size of the mismatch in regions, and the demographic structure. I
believe that relevant indicators could be calculated for all the dimensions. Such
an exercise would make the arguments much more convincing and interesting.
To address this crucial comment, which was among the most important we received, we
proceeded with major revisions on our manuscript. Specifically, following your suggestions,
we added a correlation analysis (through Pearson’s R) to our implemented methodologies.
Specifically, bivariate correlations have been conducted between the LQL, the LQM, and the
LQH on the one hand, and the national and regional GDP (total and per capita), a regional
Innovation Index by the European Commission, population density representing the level of
a region’s urbanisation, as well as the Ageing Index and the (labour force) Dependency
Index pertaining to a region’s demographic structures. The specifics of this analysis
(temporal scope, methods, data sources, interpretation approach, etc.) are laid out in detail
in the last paragraph of the Methodological Section. Then, in the Empirical Analysis section,
the correlation analysis follows the existing LQ analysis so as to contextualize its findings.

Conclusions

This study examined the issue of human capital allocation at
the regional level across five European countries, which represent key employment models within the EU. Our findings
highlighted the uneven geography of skill mismatches, as capital and metropolitan regions were observed to be more efficient

than less affluent and peripheral ones in matching supply
(in terms of education attainment level) and demand (in terms
of demanded skill-level in occupations), especially when it
comes to upper-level skills. To further decipher this remark,
we discussed the role of five interrelated factors: economic
dynamism at the national level, regional sectoral specializations, urbanization, institutional structures, and demographic
trends. In this framework, we briefly discussed the role of
regions’ positioning within broader structures such as GVCs.
Importantly, our analysis pinpointed that human capital is
shaped by multiple forces at the same time, most of which
relate with each other in a dialectical way. Furthermore, we
identified a series of self-sustained, regenerating processes of
resilience and vulnerability, i.e., virtuous and vicious cycles.
Ultimately, we found human capital to be of the utmost importance in regional development. Although it can generate spatial growth, its concentration in certain areas leaves lagging
regions out of growth pathways.
To break this pattern of uneven development, policy interventions are required. Thus, here we recommend a series of actions
drawing upon the five factors discussed above, while taking into account the EU’s “New Skills Agenda”. Our recommendations have been tailored for the regions associated with
the ERUA but can be applied to other contexts as well, given
that these regions represent Europe’s key employment regimes.
Looking at the local institutional structures and practices, in
the regions with strong research and academic activity like the
ones related to the consortium, it is important that their universities work together with stakeholders from industry to spill
over knowledge and cover the research and innovation
needs of the labour market. In this frame, learning events for
reskilling and upskilling in emerging sectors—e.g., green
skills—are necessary. In addition, high quality career counselling is key, especially for vulnerable groups such as the youth,
women, and migrants, for not only making sensible early career
decisions but also in overcoming career challenges throughout their lives (Papakota, 2016). In fact, as noted above, such
career counseling is more than necessary in peripheral regions,
where career choices are less informed due to “information
asymmetries” (McGuinness et al., 2018). In this context,
educational structures such as schools, universities or vocational training centres should respond to the needs of students
at different stages of career development by identifying skills,
experiences, values and personality traits of graduates, technological trends and employment opportunities, employers’
expectations and career planning (Litoiu & Oproiu, 2012).
Lastly, tighter networks of social, scientific, and policy-related
stakeholders should be encouraged, so that through joint
actions they engage in labour market forecasting and early
identification of skill shortages.
Regarding the spatially uneven distribution of human capital due
to national economies’ dynamism (or lack thereof) or regional
industrial specializations, it can be addressed through targeted investment incentives and guided industrial reorientation.
Governments can rechannel entrepreneurial activity into
underdeveloped regions through financial incentives like tax

breaks, grants and subsidies. More crucially, countries and
regions with economies entirely oriented towards medium and
low-skill sectors (e.g., tourism) that generate mainly low-quality
jobs, should pursue a re-specialization in more dynamic
high value-added and high-skill sectors (Emmanouil et al.,
2024); this should reduce spatial and talent inequalities. Furthermore, our analysis showed that high skills increase
inversely with population ageing and are positively associated
with the degree of urbanization; as such, investment in education, training, and continuous learning, or policies promoting economic resilience and adaptability, may not be sufficient
in rural and underdeveloped regions. This highlights the need
for a move away from a horizontal implementation of policies, which is the case with many EU initiatives such as the
Youth Guarantee (Emmanouil et al., ibid). Instead, policies
should be spatially sensitive so as to keep young people with
high levels of education in non-urban and/or peripheral regions,
where they will work in high-skill occupations and put their
human capital in good use. Taking into account the specific
needs of regions, promoting innovation, incentivizing investment, and sharing best practices, can therefore promote
balanced economic growth and reduce inequalities in the
geographical distribution of skills.

This is an improved and much more coherent version of the paper. The literature review is much
better structured, although readers should be aware that the idea of the theoretical reflection is
not to derive testable hypotheses, but to draw up the theoretical context of the paper in line with
its explorative aim. Consequently, the data analysis remains overall descriptive and illustrative of
some empirical tendencies, rather than evaluating a specific theory.

Among the most interesting empirical patters detected are those pertaining to the capital cities
and how many of these “superstar cities” produce dual results in the matching on their local
labour markets, in both ends of the labour market distribution. Many results concerning the more
peripheral region are informative too. These findings are related both to the broader literature on
within-country divergence in Europe, and the one on polarization of labour markets from a
geographical perspective.
The processes creating illustrated empirical patterns and correlations could be further discussed.
The authors themselves emphasize the ”economic dynamism at the national level, regional
industrial specializations, urbanisation levels, demographic structures, and institutional
endowments”. These indicators may themselves be correlated. On a higher level of abstraction,
the authors discuss the impact of recent decade’s regional alignment with the location structures
of global value chains. This argument resonates well with recent arguments relating to the
“geography of functions” hypothesis, but remains to be formally tested. Also, in the paper, the
mismatch issues arising in peripheral regions are largely attributed to institutional dynamics and
an information problem in these regions. These might well be factors that contribute to the
identified patterns, but given the structure of correlations, it seems to me that this is more an
issue created by the structure of regional growth (or not growth), and not so much of an issue of
information about available jobs per se.
In all, the paper gives interesting perspectives on an important regional development problem in
the EU, and its variation across regions. What could and should be done about it, apart from
implementing place-based approaches trying to facilitate general economic growth and
productive transformation, remains largely an open issue. Ultimately, it also comes down to the
opportunities that people perceive in various places, to participate in economic production and
growth. I therefore remain sceptical to general statements such as “Instead, policies should be
spatially sensitive so as to keep young people with high levels of education in non-urban and/or
peripheral regions, where they will work in high-skill occupations and put their human capital in
good use.“ Given the nature of economic dynamics nowadays, this is much easier said than done,
if we also want to keep the good features that an essentially experimental economy comes with.
